nameStory: The Lapland buttercup gets its name from Lapland, the northernmost region of Scandinavia, where this arctic wildflower was first scientifically described. Like other buttercups, it earned the 'buttercup' part of its name from the old folk belief that cows eating these flowers would produce richer, more golden butter. This tiny northern beauty brings a touch of the far arctic to New England's highest, coldest places.
description: Lapland buttercup is an extremely rare, low-growing arctic wildflower that hugs the ground with creeping underground stems. This petite plant sends up delicate yellow flowers on short stalks above deeply divided leaves that look like tiny three-fingered hands. Unlike the tall, upright buttercups you might know from meadows, this one stays prostrate and small, perfectly adapted to harsh mountain conditions. It's one of New England's rarest plants, found in only the most remote, cold, and wet locations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with typically 6 petals (sometimes 8) that are distinctly longer than the green sepals beneath them, appearing solitary on short stalks above the creeping plant

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply three-lobed leaves that feel soft and have toothed or scalloped edges, resembling tiny mittens with three fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, creeping plant that spreads by underground stems (rhizomes) and stays flat against the ground, never growing upright like other buttercups

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, forms distinctive round, globe-like clusters of small dry fruits held up on stalks above the mat of leaves

habitat: Found in New England's most remote wet, cold locations, especially in moss carpets along mountain streams, alpine lake shores, and boggy areas at high elevations. This arctic species seeks out the coldest, wettest microsites where few other flowering plants can survive. You'd only encounter it in the most pristine, undisturbed wetlands of northern New England's highest peaks.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early from underground stems as snow melts, forming small mats of fresh green three-lobed foliage in wet, mossy areas.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom on short stalks above the leaf mats, followed by the distinctive globe-shaped seed heads that rise above the creeping plant.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may persist into early fall, gradually dying back as temperatures drop and the growing season ends in these harsh mountain locations.
seasonality.winter: Plant retreats completely underground, surviving winter through its creeping rhizome system buried safely beneath snow and frozen soil.

funFact: With only 3 recorded observations in all of New England, you're statistically more likely to spot a moose than this tiny wildflower - making it one of our region's most elusive botanical treasures that most botanists never see in their entire careers!
confusionNotes: The prostrate, creeping growth habit and 6-petaled flowers distinguish it from all other New England buttercups, which grow upright and typically have 5 petals. If you find a buttercup hugging the ground in a wet, mossy arctic environment, you've likely found something very special.
contextualKnowledge: This is an arctic-alpine relict species, meaning it's a survivor from the last ice age that retreated to the coldest, most remote spots as the climate warmed. Finding one would be a significant botanical discovery worth reporting to local naturalist organizations.
compareHints: Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping. While other buttercups typically have 5 petals, this species usually has 6, and its habitat in wet moss carpets at high elevations is unlike any other regional buttercup. Most related species prefer meadows, fields, or regular wetlands rather than these extreme arctic-like conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
